doc.title: Jimmy Lewis interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Teaching himself the bass from a Bob Haggart book
summary: Told the club wants a bass, he buys one, learns from a book and plays everything on one string; ukulele helped his tone and chords.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: On ukulele. At the end of the year he says, “everybody keeps asking about a bass fiddle.” He said, “You don’t have one of these.” So I said uh oh, they’re going to get rid of me and get a bass. So what I did, I went down the next day to a place and got me a bass. I brought it home, didn’t know anything about it. Had it tuned, had a man in the store tune it up, and the first string, the G string, I could play everything on the G string. It’s one string, right here. And so I got my book, I think one of these Bob Haggart books. And I stayed in that book for about six months. And I came out playing better than anybody in the town. I taught myself.
Well I think your ukulele playing must have helped.

Yeah, it was for tone you know, and sound, chords and all that. So I went back, took the bass to the club that night, and the guy was surprised to see me walk in with a bass you know. I took my ukulele too in case it didn’t work out. So I played, you know he called the tunes and I played everything by ear, everything in tune and everything, but on one string. At that time you used to use the gut strings on the bass. And so I’d wear out a string a week. Every week I had to get a new G string. The other strings —
